overview: Akwẽ is a self-name of the Xerente, a Jê-speaking Indigenous people of the Tocantins region of Brazil. This entry concerns Xerente communities near Tocantínia, between the Tocantins and Sono rivers. Their relationships with the Xavante and Xakriabá do not make these distinct peoples interchangeable.

periods.title: Colonial settlements and resistance
periods.summary: Portuguese authorities attempted to concentrate Indigenous people in settlements during the later eighteenth century. Resistance and departures frustrated these policies. This was a struggle over territory and control, not the founding of the Xerente people.

periods.title: Demarcation and continuing territorial struggles
periods.summary: In 1972 the Xerente obtained demarcation of the territory known as Área Grande. Recognition followed prolonged conflict over their lands; it did not restore the full extent of their earlier territory.

periods.title: Community organizations and land management
periods.summary: The Xerente brigade association ABIX formed in October 2014. Its work connected community organization, knowledge of fire, plant propagation and partnerships with environmental institutions. The GATI report records projects undertaken in 2015 to 2016.

sections.title: A basket, its materials and its geometry

items.text: A golden-grass basket given to researcher Elisângela Melo during fieldwork in 2006 later became the subject of Wesley Coelho de Sousa’s mathematics study. Its known history is a gift and a research collection, not an archaeological excavation. The basket’s maker is not named in the account.

The studied basket has bundled golden-grass fibers joined with fine buriti-palm fiber. Its tightly coiled base supports open sides with repeated triangular forms and a firm rim. The different arrangements of the same materials produce both a containing surface and a visible decorative structure.

Sousa used the basket to explore geometric forms and possibilities for mathematics teaching. Pandemic restrictions prevented interviews with its makers. His analysis of shapes therefore cannot establish the maker’s own terminology, intentions or mathematical explanations. It remains an interpretation of a particular object.

Fieldwork in Porteira and Funil in 2013 to 2014 recorded adobe houses with palm roofing. Sleeping and living rooms occupied one small building, while cooking occupied another; washing facilities stood outside. This household arrangement connected shelter, food preparation and surrounding yards.

The same study observed refrigerators, stoves and other electrical appliances, alongside some continued wood-fire cooking. Instant noodles, powdered drinks and packaged biscuits appeared among purchased foods. These observations describe changing household practices in the two studied villages, rather than a timeless menu for all Xerente people.

Some households continued growing cassava, yams and pigeon peas. Residents described hunting peccaries, deer and armadillos; researchers also recorded craft production as a source of income. Cultivation, hunting, making goods and buying food formed overlapping livelihoods.

In interviews during 2019 to 2020, people described sharing large hunted animals among hunters and then their relatives. The researchers observed particular care to include elders. Food distribution expressed social obligations as well as meeting household needs.

Dona Pizadi of Salto recalled communal planting and harvest gatherings with shared food and singing. Other participants described more recent family plots and home gardens. Valcir Sinã connected difficulties with riverbank cultivation to changed water levels below the hydroelectric dam. These attributed accounts record change without declaring farming extinct.

sections.title: Social knowledge and caring for land

items.text: Ethnographic accounts describe the Doí and Wahirê social divisions, connected by reciprocal duties and clan relationships. Circular and linear body-painting motifs identify affiliations. Designs applied with carved buriti-pith stamps show how knowledge of materials and visual forms can communicate a person’s place in social life.

The GATI report describes ABIX working with Ibama’s Prevfogo program to combine Xerente fire knowledge with environmental management. Participants mapped vulnerable areas, forests, wildlife refuges and wetlands containing golden grass. This was a specific collaborative project, not evidence that every fire or ecological problem had been controlled.

ABIX also established a plant nursery at Funai’s Tocantínia site. Seedlings were intended for restoring cleared areas and for household fruit gardens. The report connects nursery work with exchanges and training, including agricultural projects in 2015 to 2016, showing land care as organized community work.

ending.text: Xerente communities continue to transmit knowledge and adapt their livelihoods. The 2019 to 2020 fieldwork records living participants debating changes in hunting, farming and food sharing. Territorial losses and environmental pressures are real, but the map’s endpoint in 1500 is not a supported extinction date or the fall of a Xerente state.
